title: Design a URL Shortener

Consider TTL for temporary URLs

title: Design a Distributed Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
question: Design a precise sliding-window rate limiter for a multi-region API: 1000 requests/minute per API key, exact window semantics, clock skew across regions, tiered limits (free vs paid).
mental_model: Per-key sorted timestamp logs in Redis; exact window counts; tier config drives limits; edge enforcement.

solution.approach: Sliding-window log per key in Redis (ZADD timestamps, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE expiry). Count in window decides allow/deny. Tier config sets window/limit per plan.

explanation: Sliding-window logs give exact window semantics at O(window) memory, unlike fixed windows with boundary spikes. Regional Redis keeps decisions local; async reconciliation heals cross-region double-spend. Tiers are config, not code branches.
hints: Sorted sets make window expiry a single range-delete
Exactness costs memory: 1000 timestamps per key
Clock skew matters only at window edges — bound it, don't eliminate it
Tiers belong in config so limits change without deploys
common_trap: Fixed-window counters allow 2x bursts at boundaries (end of one window + start of next). Sliding windows exist precisely to close that hole.
reasoning_steps: 2. Reject fixed window (boundary bursts) with the 2x math
3. Design per-key sorted timestamp logs in Redis
4. Handle clock skew with NTP bounds + reconciliation
constraints: 1000 req/min per key, exact window, <5ms overhead, multi-region clock skew, tiered limits
follow_up: How would you implement different rate limits for different user tiers? Pressure: two regions disagree about a key by 40 requests — who wins, and what does the customer see?
statement: Design a sliding-window rate limiter for a multi-region public API: exact 1000 req/min per key semantics, region clock skew, and per-tier limits.
scale_estimation: Sliding-window log keeps ~1000 timestamps/key (~16KB); 1M active keys ~= 16GB across the fleet. Cross-region sync is the cost center — NTP bounds skew to ~100ms; decisions use local region state with async reconciliation.

title: Design a Write-Through Distributed Cache
question: Design a write-through distributed cache for a read-heavy catalog: 1M QPS reads, 10K QPS writes, hot-key skew, thundering-herd protection.
mental_model: Writes go through cache to DB synchronously; reads never see stale data beyond TTL; hot keys are replicated, not sharded.

solution.approach: Write-through writer persists to DB on every write before ack. Read-through proxy loads misses from DB. Hot-key detector replicates top keys. Request coalescing collapses stampedes.

explanation: Write-through trades write latency for read freshness — right at 100:1 read dominance. Hot-key splitting fixes the skew that consistent hashing alone cannot. Coalescing turns 10K simultaneous miss-storms into 1 DB read.
hints: Write-through is cheap exactly when reads dominate writes
Hot keys break even perfect hashing — replicate them
Coalesce concurrent misses into one backend read
Warm the cache before cutover, not after
common_trap: Cache-aside with TTL-only expiry serves stale catalog prices after writes. Write-through closes that window by construction.
reasoning_steps: 1. Clarify read/write ratio, freshness needs, hot-key reality
2. Choose write-through for freshness at 100:1 reads
constraints: 1M read QPS, 10K write QPS, <1ms p99 reads, hot-key skew, cold-start survival
follow_up: How would you handle cache invalidation? Prevent cache stampede? Pressure: the DB primary lags 30 seconds behind writes — what do readers see, and who notices first?
statement: Design a write-through cache for a read-heavy catalog: 1M read QPS, 10K write QPS, skewed hot keys, thundering-herd protection.
scale_estimation: Read:write = 100:1, so write-through cost is negligible (~10K/sec) while guaranteeing freshness. Hot keys: top 0.01% of keys take ~50% of reads — replicate hot keys across N nodes or split by suffix. Cold start: warming job replays yesterday's hot set before cutover.
